compounding_issues: Session 1 hit a hard provider rate limit ('You've hit your session limit', resets 7:30am Europe/Berlin) and produced no code; every subsequent session inherited the same blocked state, so sessions 2-5 had no partial work to build on and failed identically.
The framework committed 3-line .instrument/session_N.jsonl error transcripts as each session's 'feature' commit, so the git history implies a progression that does not exist in the code.
No retry, backoff, or abort logic triggered across 5 consecutive rate-limited sessions — the run burned all 5 sessions on a condition it should have detected after session 1.

The seed codebase is a mismatched generic NestJS-like Auth API (tier2_small/good), not an SSG, so even under a working model the agent would have faced a poor architectural starting point for static_site_gen.
No accumulation of tests, code, or architecture occurred, so there was nothing for later sessions to refactor, integrate, or extend.
key_decisions: Task-type sequencing (greenfield -> feature_addition -> integration -> refactor -> cross_cutting) was a sound capstone plan; incremental-build caching in session 5 is the natural finale for an SSG — but it was never realized.
Running the story under a model that was already at its daily session cap, with no early-abort guard, so all 5 sessions uniformly failed before any reasoning token was spent.
Reusing the tier2_small/good seed as-is despite its domain mismatch with the static site generator task.
Committing instrumentation-only sessions into the story git history rather than skipping/failing fast, which later inflates review/analysis passes that see 'no changes'.
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality was flat and void across all five sessions: each commit is an empty transcript recording the same rate-limit error, with zero code, zero tokens, zero tests, and exit code 1. There was no improvement or degradation arc because implementation never began — session 1 did not start and sessions 2-5 could not, so the 'trajectory' is a constant failure plateau rather than a rising or decaying quality curve. The only signal of motion is the nominal task labels in the commit messages, which describe a coherent SSG build plan that the codebase never actually received.
story_review.summary: A nominally well-planned five-session SSG progression that produced zero code — every session was blocked by a provider rate limit and committed only an error transcript, so the history is empty scaffolding with no implementation to evaluate.
